newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: No sign of survivors in Australia ski resort ruins.
newsitem.headline: No sign of survivors in Australia ski resort ruins.

text.p: Rescuers searching for up to 20 people buried in the ruins of two Australian ski lodges destroyed in a landslide said on Thursday there were no signs of life in the wreckage.
But as darkness fell in the Snowy Mountains and temperatures plummeted below freezing, rescuers using arc lights said they would search through the night for survivors.
"There were no signs of life at all. There is still hope but one has to be honest, that hope is diminishing," said regional police commander Bruce Johnston.
The landslide hit the Thredbo Alpine Village, in the Snowy Mountains, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney, just before midnight on Wednesday.
Tonnes of soil, rocks and gum trees crushed the Carinya lodge, which contained one person, sending it cascading onto the Bimbadeen lodge, which contained up to 19 people -- including Americans.
In Tokyo, Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Thursday he planned to cut short a trade promotion trip to visit the site of the landslide.
Fischer said he would attend talks with Japanese ministers on Friday and return to Australia on Saturday, cancelling a scheduled climb of Mount Fuji.
In Thredbo, rescuers were unable to launch an immediate full-scale search for survivors as the site was dangerously unstable, with more landslides feared, police said.
But 17 hours after the landslide, Johnston said rescuers had reported that they had found no signs of life after probing the rubble with fibre-optic cameras and thermal imaging equipment.
"Unfortunately we have had negative results with both those techniques," he said. "There were cries that were heard very soon after the slippage, but nothing has been heard since."
In this close-knit village, where many know the people trapped, rescuers were not giving up hope of finding survivors.
Light snow dusted a human chain of rescuers who sifted by hand through the twisted ruins of the lodges, unable to use earth moving equipment for fear of more landslides.
Witnesses said the landslide sounded like a big gust of wind that shook the lodges perched on the side of the mountain.
"We just heard this enormous rush like I'd imagine you'd experience with a tornado just hitting a building...," said Glenn Milne, who was holidaying in an adjacent lodge.
Immediately after the landslide, anti-theft alarms from buried cars sounded from beneath the rubble.
Milne said residents in nearby lodges rushed to the collapsed buildings and began frantically digging in the rubble to reach survivors in the freezing, dark night.
"We got down into the rubble and we started clawing away chunks of rubble," Milne said.
"When the lodges collapsed, cars also came down on top -- they were teetering on the edge of the rubble. Every time we moved chunks of rubble, the cars were unstable at the top."
The landslide occurred just before midnight at a time when Thredbo, at an altitude of 1,370 metres (4,494 feet), was packed with thousands of Australian and foreign visitors.
Thredbo sits on a ridge facing the snow-covered mountain range of the Kosciuszko National Park, which rises to 2,037 metres (6,683 feet).
Australia's ski season runs from June to October but has started slowly this year as little snow has fallen on the village.
Police believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way, sending tonnes of dirt, rock and trees crashing onto the lodges.
Lodges further down the slope escaped the landslide, allowing rescuers easy road access to the scene and for evacuations.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.
"It reminds me of looking at a picture of a tornado site or something where it's just cleaned a path through and on either side there is no damage whatsoever," he said.
